The power grid just became the AI bottleneck. The Information reports Mississippi's Entergy told Amazon it would start kicking Amazon's data centers off the grid at peak times, a previously unreported warning that prompted AWS to change how those sites switch to backup power.

Amazon's answer is Project Falcon. Now the utility can switch the sites to backup power on its own, without contacting AWS. Falcon was built for Mississippi and may roll out elsewhere in the U.S. As Synergetic CEO Mike Sloan put it: "[Data centers] have to accept some curtailment, which means then the data center has to have a toolbox that can handle that risk."

Energy will be the biggest problem in AI/data centers. There's no doubt about that. And the outdated grid has to handle this overload. That's hundreds of billions that haven't even been factored in yet.
Source: https://t.co/yPchMxzbaO

Andrej Karpathy’s point: Many people only use AI occasionally for search or writing and see little value in their daily lives. Even many professionals understand its progress mainly in theory. 

People using advanced models extensively for coding and math experience huge capability gains, widening the gap in how people perceive AI.

And this impression has been confirmed here in Paris during my trip. When I talk to people, I realize they're completely unaware of how capable AI already is. They're unaware of the possibilities it offers. They haven't heard that OpenAI solved a Millennium Prize problem, or recently solved 372 math problems, some of which had remained unsolved for decades.

Currently, we're living in an ivory tower.

I think this is one of the most important graphs of the last few months, and perhaps years. For a long time, there was speculation about how AI would affect the labor market.

Clearly, it was only a matter of time before AI reached the white-collar sector, but empirical evidence was scarce, ultimately because, of course, one only really understands how the market situation develops in retrospect.

Now, as in this example, we see that AI is clearly and unequivocally entering certain professions and replacing people. Call center agents are the first to be replaced. And as more AI and agents enter the workforce, a similar process will spread to other areas of work. Frankly, I don't believe that AI will necessarily create new jobs, resulting in a net zero. I think more jobs will be replaced than created. This needs to be discussed.

Yes, computing remains a bottleneck, and demand massively exceeds supply. But far more crucial is being able to power the data centers. China is currently building 38 new nuclear reactors with a combined capacity of approximately 39.8 gigawatts. The US, on the other hand, is primarily focusing on small nuclear reactors for the future. And that's not even mentioning solar capacity.

Seriously: the future will be decided by energy. By grid expansion, energy production, and scaling. And China has a clear lead here.

Today I had the pleasure of interviewing Shruti Koparkar from @NVIDIA, who focuses on accelerated computing and AI inference.

We talked about CUDA and CUDA-X, the economics of AI infrastructure, and how long GPUs can remain useful and profitable as models and workloads change.

When does it make sense to keep using an older GPU system? When should you repurpose it or replace it? And what role does software play in that decision?

It was a real pleasure discussing these questions with Shruti. Thank you for your time and the conversation!

We’ll be uploading the full interview soon. I’m really looking forward to sharing it with you, but wanted to share a first update today. 🙂

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
